content: The Gemini observatory needs an integrated software environment for controlling its telescopes and scientific instruments. Observing astronomers should be able to acquire astronomical data and assess its quality without having to manage the low-level details of individual subsystems. The system must support users with different operational responsibilities and provide consistent access to telescope status and observing functions from appropriate local or remote facilities.

The main goal is to let astronomers collect scientifically useful data from the telescope without getting bogged down in the mechanics of the instruments and control subsystems. In business terms, it should improve observing efficiency, reduce operator burden, and help ensure that time on the telescope produces high-quality results.
During a typical session, the value comes from giving the observing team a single, reliable way to point, configure, monitor, and assess the observation as it happens. They should be able to see whether the telescope and instruments are behaving correctly, judge data quality quickly, and adjust the plan if conditions or results aren’t meeting expectations.

Beyond just getting data and checking quality, we want the session to produce usable scientific results with minimal wasted telescope time. That means the observation should be executed safely and efficiently, the right instrument setup should be achieved, and the astronomer should leave with confidence that the intended target and exposure sequence were actually completed. If conditions change, the system should also support quick recovery or adjustment so the night can stay productive.

The most critical capabilities are accurate telescope control, reliable instrument configuration, and real-time status and quality feedback, because if any of those fail the night can be lost or the data can be unusable. After that comes the ability to adapt quickly to changing conditions and keep the workflow simple for the observer so time isn’t wasted on operational complexity. Things like convenience features are useful, but they matter less than safety, correctness, and steady observing throughput.

The hardest situations are usually when the session has to switch quickly between targets or observing modes, especially if the instrument setup is complex or the previous configuration wasn’t fully cleared. Problems also come up when weather, seeing, or tracking conditions change and the team has to react fast without making a mistake. In practice, anything that forces people to manage several subsystems manually at once increases the chance of delay or configuration error.

They should not have to deal with the individual device protocols, hardware registers, timing sequences, or all the separate steps needed to move motors, switch filters, or synchronize exposures. They also shouldn’t need to manage the underlying safety interlocks, network connections, or low-level error recovery for each subsystem. The idea is to give them a single observing interface that presents the telescope and instruments in terms of what they want to do, not how the hardware happens to do it.

Usually the observing astronomer decides what the next observing action should be, based on the science plan and what the telescope is showing them. An operator or control system then carries it out, with the system enforcing the safe and valid sequence of steps. The fit with everyone else is that the astronomer focuses on the science decision, while the support staff and automation handle execution, safety, and coordination with the telescope subsystems.

The instrument specialist is there to make sure the instrument is set up correctly and that any unusual change is technically safe and likely to work. If the observing sequence has to be adjusted quickly, they help interpret whether the change is feasible, whether the instrument needs reconfiguration, and whether the resulting data will still be scientifically valid. They also tend to be the person who can troubleshoot instrument-specific issues faster than the observing astronomer or general operator.

The most important shared meanings are the current telescope state, instrument state, target, observing mode, and whether the data quality is acceptable or not. People also need to understand the same terms for readiness, pause, abort, and recover, because those actions have to mean the same thing to everyone in the room. If those words are not interpreted consistently, the whole session can drift or someone can make the wrong move at the wrong time.

Readiness means the telescope and instrument are fully in a safe, configured state and the next observing action can proceed without hidden dependencies. Pause is used when you need to stop before the next exposure or motion because conditions are changing, but nothing unsafe is happening; abort is for when continuing would risk bad data or equipment safety, so the current action should stop immediately. Recover is used after a pause or abort once the system is back in a known-good state, and if someone tries any of these in an unexpected state, the system should refuse the action, explain why, and show what state it is actually in so the team can correct course.

Typically we start by confirming the telescope and instrument are in a known safe state, then we load or verify the instrument configuration and slew to the target. After that we acquire the target, fine-tune the pointing or focus if needed, and begin the exposure or observing sequence. Once data is taken, we check basic quality, decide whether to repeat or adjust, and then either continue with the next target or wrap up the session and stow the system safely.

Yes, there should be clear operational criteria for that. A session is only officially started once the necessary setup, authorization, and system readiness checks are complete, and it ends when observing is finished and the telescope and instruments are placed in their required safe state. If those conditions are not fully met, the system should not mark the session as started or ended; it should stay in the current status and tell the operator what is still missing.

The main triggers are things like a new target being selected, a change in observing mode, a command to start or stop an exposure, a quality check failing, or a condition change such as weather or tracking drift. When those events occur, the system should respond automatically where possible by moving to the next safe step, or otherwise present a clear status and require operator confirmation. In general, each event should cause the system to either execute the observing action, pause it, or protect the hardware and data quality if the situation is no longer acceptable.

Manual changes should be limited to the people responsible for that subsystem, usually the instrument specialist for instrument settings and the telescope operator for telescope-related adjustments. The order should follow the dependency chain, so safety and basic configuration come first, then pointing and instrument setup, and only then the observing action itself. The system should stop and ask for confirmation whenever a change could affect safety, invalidate the current configuration, or introduce a delay that might make the sequence inconsistent with the planned observation.

A manual change can proceed without confirmation only when it is clearly low risk, reversible, and does not affect the current exposure, telescope motion, or instrument state in any meaningful way. An acceptable override would usually be something like correcting a minor display or metadata issue, or making a pre-approved tweak that the current operator role is explicitly allowed to do. If there is any chance the change could alter the observing result, interfere with safety, or break the planned sequence, then it should require a stop and confirmation.

The main products are the raw science exposures, the associated calibration frames, and the basic metadata that tells us how each exposure was taken, along with a quick-look assessment of quality. Those need to be preserved so astronomers can verify the observation, compare it against the intended setup, and later pass it into reduction or archive processes. In the workflow, the system should capture them automatically during observing and make them available immediately enough for the team to decide whether to continue, repeat, or adjust the next observation.

Yes, that responsibility can shift, but only under controlled conditions. Normally the subsystem owner or designated operator makes the change, but if they’re unavailable or the observation is time-critical, a qualified backup role can step in as long as they have the proper access and the shift is recorded for accountability. If the backup isn’t explicitly authorized, then the system should hold the change and require escalation rather than letting someone else proceed informally.

The rule should be that a later step can proceed only if the prerequisite step is already complete and verified, or if the system can safely and explicitly validate that dependency right then. If the prerequisite is not satisfied and can be completed in time, the system should pause and wait for it; if it cannot be satisfied without risking the observing window or configuration integrity, it should block the change and escalate to the operator. The main priority is to avoid applying a dependent change against an uncertain state.

I’d accept an override without confirmation only for minor, low-risk adjustments that don’t affect the active exposure or hardware motion, like correcting a non-operational setting, fixing a labeling error, or applying a pre-approved housekeeping change. I’d draw the line anywhere the change could alter the observing result, disturb tracking, touch safety-related controls, or invalidate the current configuration. If there’s any doubt about impact, it should stop and require operator approval.

Yes, remotely operated sessions should be more conservative because there’s less immediate physical oversight. If staffing is reduced or the on-site response is delayed, the system should limit manual changes to pre-authorized actions and prefer automated safeguards or deferred execution rather than letting operators force risky adjustments. If direct oversight is lost altogether, then any nonessential change should be blocked until communication and authority are restored.

If it can be translated safely and unambiguously, the system should handle the low-level steps automatically so the observer doesn’t have to manage subsystem details. If the request is ambiguous, risky, or requires judgment about the telescope or instrument state, then it should be routed to an operator rather than rejected outright, because we still want a path to get it done when appropriate. Only if it cannot be mapped to a valid observing operation at all should the system reject it as too technical.

In practice, the observing operator or night operator should take over if the instrument specialist can’t resolve it in time, because they’re the ones responsible for keeping the session moving safely. The sequence should be paused if the issue affects data quality, configuration, or hardware safety, and deferred if the fix would consume more time than the current observing slot can tolerate. It should only resume once the state is confirmed healthy and the operator agrees the next step is safe to continue.

Yes, there should be warning thresholds for things like unstable tracking, instrument status faults, or a configuration mismatch, and any of those should trigger an automatic pause before the next step. If the condition is borderline rather than outright failed, the system should warn the operator and require approval before continuing. Anything that touches hardware safety should be treated as a hard stop until it’s cleared.

On a typical night, the system should support getting the telescope ready, loading the planned observing sequence, acquiring targets, checking data quality as you go, and switching instruments or configurations without forcing observers to deal with subsystem details. Operationally, the goal is to keep the night moving smoothly while giving operators clear visibility into status, warnings, and any exceptions that need intervention. It should fit into the normal flow by letting observers work from one consistent interface and letting operators step in only when a change needs approval, a fault appears, or the sequence has to be paused or recovered.

It should transition gradually, not as a hard cutover, because we can’t afford to disrupt ongoing observing. Existing control practices need to keep working during the changeover, and sessions already in progress should be allowed to finish under the current mode unless there’s a safety reason to stop them. Observers and operators will need a clear handoff period with training and a defined point where the new interface becomes the normal path for starting and running sessions.

I would expect it to handle new telescope configurations, upgraded detectors, different spectrographs or imagers, and probably additional calibration and monitoring services as the observatory grows. The main expectation is that we shouldn’t have to redesign the whole control environment every time a subsystem changes. It should be flexible enough to add or replace instruments and supporting services without breaking the common observing workflow.

That would usually fall to the observatory software and operations support team, working closely with the instrument specialists and operators who know the subsystem details. Changes should be introduced through a staged process with testing in a non-operational environment first, then a planned deployment window, and only after that should they be enabled for normal observing. If anything affects active sessions, it should be deferred until the current night is safe to hand over or paused only if there’s a compelling operational reason.

If the new setup fits the same basic observing pattern and only changes parameters, mappings, or supported limits, then a configuration update should be enough. If it changes how observers acquire targets, manage exposures, switch instruments, or check quality in a meaningful way, then the workflow needs a more substantial change. In general, anything that affects the operator handoff, approvals, or safety checks should be treated as a workflow change rather than just a config tweak.

The operator should see enough status to know what the system is doing, whether a subsystem is healthy, busy, delayed, or unavailable, and what part of the observing flow is affected. The low-level interaction details should stay hidden unless the operator needs them to diagnose a problem or approve a fallback action. If a service is slow or errors out, the interface should present a clear operational state and the next safe option, rather than exposing raw technical noise.

If the change could interrupt an active exposure, alter telescope motion, affect safety limits, or invalidate the current observing sequence, it should wait until the night is safe. If it’s a contained update that has already been tested and only needs a planned switch-over with no impact on active work, then it can be enabled sooner in a controlled window. The deciding factor is whether the change can be made without risking the current session or forcing operators into an unplanned recovery.

If the new configuration can use the same observing steps, status model, and operator controls with just added parameters or device-specific translations, it should be a plug-in extension. If it introduces a different sequence of actions, new timing constraints, or a different way of assessing data quality, then it needs a dedicated adaptation so we don’t force everyone into an awkward workaround. The key is preserving a consistent observing workflow for astronomers and operators while still letting the subsystem behave correctly.

I’d treat it as a dedicated adaptation if it needs its own safety interlocks, a different command sequence, or special handling for failures that doesn’t match the standard telescope and instrument flow. The same goes for boundary cases like long-running asynchronous actions, multiple concurrent states, or a service that can partially succeed and leave the system in an ambiguous condition. If operators have to think about it differently to use it safely, it’s probably more than a plug-in.

Yes, some data should be restricted when it could expose sensitive operational details, proprietary observing programs, or access-limited engineering information. In live operations, we’d usually want observers to see the data and status they need for the current session, but mask anything that belongs to another program or to restricted technical diagnostics unless they’re authorized. If there’s a security concern or a proprietary period, then delay or concealment may be necessary, but I’d want the exact policy confirmed with operations and data management.

A session should only start when the required setup is complete, the needed authorization is in place, and the readiness checks all come back clean, including telescope, instrument, and safety status. If any critical item is incomplete or the system is in an unsafe or ambiguous state, we should hold the start until it’s resolved. Ending a session is similar: it should be allowed when the current observation is complete or when an operator needs to stop for safety, failure recovery, or an approved handoff.

We should record status changes that affect observing decisions, safety, data quality, or any handoff between operators or sessions. Routine internal churn probably doesn’t need every single transition if it doesn’t change what the operator sees or does, but anything that explains a pause, failure, recovery, or configuration change should be kept. Safety events, fault conditions, command rejections, and state changes that affect an exposure or telescope motion should always be logged.

We should capture transitions that change where the telescope is pointed, what target or mode is active, why a slew or offset was commanded, and any state change tied to exposure start, pause, resume, abort, or recovery. It’s also important to log transitions caused by safety limits, operator intervention, or a subsystem fault, because those explain the reason behind the change. I’d leave out very fine-grained internal updates that don’t alter the observing state in a meaningful way, like repeated heartbeat-style updates or minor implementation-level retries that never became visible to operators.

In an active session, operators and the assigned observing team should be able to view the live telemetry and the data needed to run the observation, but only if they’re properly authorized for that program or facility. Copying or exporting should be limited to users with the right role and permission, especially for raw data, engineering telemetry, or anything under a proprietary period. If a user isn’t authorized, or if the information belongs to another program or reveals restricted diagnostics, it should be masked or withheld rather than partially exposed.

The default should be that they only see the current program’s information, because that’s what they need to operate the session safely and efficiently. Cross-program data, deeper diagnostics, or partially restricted details should only appear if the user’s role explicitly calls for it and they’re cleared for that level of access. If there’s any doubt, I’d rather hide it than risk showing something they shouldn’t see.

They should stay as consistent as possible throughout the system. If the same action appears in different functions, users should not have to relearn what it means or worry that it behaves differently unless there is a very clear operational reason, like safety interlocks or a role restriction. Any exception should be rare and explicit, because inconsistency in a telescope control environment can easily cause mistakes.

If the required state is not met, the safest default is to block it outright and tell the user why. Queuing should only be used when the operation is explicitly designed to wait for a later state and we’ve agreed that’s safe and predictable, otherwise it can create surprises. Allowing it with just a warning feels too risky for this kind of system unless it’s a very low-impact action.

For remote observing, feedback needs to feel near real-time for the operator to trust it, especially for motion, exposure state, and any safety-related conditions. If the delay starts stretching beyond a couple of seconds, it becomes hard to make good decisions and harder to tell whether a command actually took effect. For less critical status updates, a bit more delay is tolerable, but the core control loop should stay very responsive.

Yes, we would want to preserve useful auxiliary products like quick-look quality assessments, reduced previews, acquisition images, and session logs when they help explain what happened or support later review. Anything that is purely transient and not useful for science, troubleshooting, or audit purposes can be discarded. If a derived product is used to make an operational decision or to document the state of the session, I’d keep it.

If the product is needed to reconstruct the observation, support data quality review, or document a decision made during the session, it should be part of the official record. That includes things like the final acquisition image, quality metrics tied to the exposure, and any log or status snapshot that explains an important event. Temporary scratch files, intermediate processing steps, or previews that are replaced by a later definitive product can be treated as working output and discarded.
